assessment:
In this study, Schulte and colleagues explore an innovative approach to characterize antigen-specific antibody repertoires by integrating cryo-electron microscopy (cryoEM) with mass spectrometry-based proteomics. The authors aim to simultaneously determine antibody sequences and map epitopes directly from secreted antibodies in biological fluids, addressing a key limitation of current methods that rely on peripheral blood memory B-cells, which may not fully represent the circulating antibody repertoire. This work is motivated by the need to understand antibody-mediated immunity at the molecular level, including the precise sequences and structural details of antibody-antigen interactions.

The authors assembled a comprehensive benchmark of 164 cryoEM maps of monoclonal antibody-antigen complexes from the Electron Microscopy Data Bank and used the deep-learning tool ModelAngelo to generate de novo atomic models without prior sequence information. They adapted their previously developed software Stitch to consolidate fragmented ModelAngelo outputs into consensus antibody sequences and evaluate V-gene assignments. The key findings demonstrate that while map quality is a critical bottleneck, antibody variable domains can be sequenced from cryoEM reconstructions with accuracies reaching 80-90% for high-quality maps. Although the ~15% error rate exceeds typical somatic hypermutation levels (1-10%), the ModelAngelo-derived sequences successfully identify the correct V-genes with significantly higher accuracy than random selection (mean/median identities of 0.78/0.87 for heavy chains and 0.75/0.85 for light chains, improving to 0.89/1.00 at higher alignment score cutoffs). The authors provide a compelling proof-of-principle using the CR3022 antibody, demonstrating that ModelAngelo-derived templates improve LC-MS/MS-based sequence assembly accuracy to 96-99% and critically enhance tolerance to complex polyclonal backgrounds.

The evidence supporting the main claims is solid and appropriately validated. The benchmark analysis is comprehensive with 152 maps analyzed and includes proper statistical testing (Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests, p<0.0001). The CR3022 case study effectively demonstrates the practical utility of the integrated approach, particularly in handling background antibody mixtures where accuracy drops below 0.6 with MS alone but recovers to >0.95 with ModelAngelo-derived templates. The analysis of 46 published EMPEM maps shows that approximately one-third yield sufficient quality for V-gene inference, with 8 maps achieving alignment scores >50 corresponding to estimated V-gene identities of ~0.85/0.90. However, this extrapolation to EMPEM data lacks independent validation with known sequences, representing a limitation. The authors appropriately acknowledge that global FSC resolution is a poor predictor of sequencing success, likely because it reflects the bulk antigen rather than local resolution in the epitope-paratope region. Additional limitations include modest CDR3 coverage (66-68 maps) and the speculative nature of claims about current method limitations (1-10 antibody depth).

This work makes an important contribution to the field by demonstrating the feasibility of integrating structural and proteomic approaches for antibody repertoire characterization. The method addresses critical gaps in current approaches, particularly heavy-light chain pairing (preserved in cryoEM but lost in proteomics) and provides a path toward characterizing the functionally relevant serum antibody compartment. While the pure sequencing accuracy from cryoEM alone is insufficient for direct antibody reconstruction, the successful V-gene identification and improved MS-based assembly demonstrate practical utility. The findings will be of significant interest to researchers in structural immunology, antibody discovery, and vaccine development, though further work is needed to establish throughput, validate EMPEM-derived sequences, and determine the true depth of repertoire coverage achievable with these methods.
